planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in gritty, fast-draining, alkaline soil in full sun; littleleaf cordia resents heavy clay or poorly drained beds and performs best in raised or rocky sites typical of South Texas caliche.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, alkaline, fast-draining soil; littleleaf cordia is a fine-textured, densely branched shrub from the Chihuahuan Desert and South Texas brush country prized for its small, felty gray-green leaves and papery white flowers that open in flushes after summer rains and fade to a soft lavender-blue by evening. The crepe-textured blooms draw bees and small butterflies throughout the warm season and the plant's naturally rounded, twiggy form needs little pruning to stay tidy. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant and handle reflected heat, poor soil, and caliche far better than moist or fertile beds, making this a low-input choice for xeric borders and rock gardens. It tolerates brief dips into the low 20s F but benefits from a warm microclimate and excellent drainage at the northern edge of zone 8b.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension -- Earth-Kind Landscaping
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after all frost danger has passed, in well-drained sandy or loamy soil in full sun to light shade; bloodberry is cold-sensitive and best sited in a protected, warm spot at the northern edge of its range.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; bloodberry is a rough-leaved, densely twiggy Florida and Caribbean native shrub whose small clusters of white to pale lavender flowers open nearly year-round in frost-free weather and are visited by tiny native bees and skipper butterflies. The blooms give way to shiny orange-red berries that songbirds seek out, and the foliage serves as a larval host for several small moth species, making the shrub a quiet but steady contributor to a wildlife garden. It is naturally compact and shrubby, tolerates sandy and slightly saline soils, and needs only light pruning to maintain a neat mounded form. Because it is more cold-sensitive than most of the shrubs in this collection, plant it against a south-facing wall or in a sheltered courtyard in zone 9a and expect dieback in hard freezes with recovery from the base.
sources: Florida Native Plant Society -- Cordia globosa profile
Institute for Regional Conservation -- Natives For Your Neighborhood

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9 this hybrid coral tree freezes to the ground most winters but resprouts reliably from the crown and blooms the same season on new growth, behaving as a large die-back perennial rather than a woody tree.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Bidwill's coral tree is a garden hybrid of Erythrina crista-galli and the native Erythrina herbacea, combining the taller, repeat-blooming flower spikes of crista-galli with a more compact, shrubbier habit better suited to smaller Gulf Coast gardens. Long, deep-pink to red spikes rise above the foliage from late spring through fall, drawing hummingbirds throughout the growing season, and the thorny stems benefit from being cut back hard each winter regardless of frost damage to encourage vigorous new flowering growth. It thrives in the same sandy, well-drained conditions as its parent species and tolerates brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s F at the root zone even when top growth is lost. Because it rarely sets viable seed, plants are propagated from cuttings, so source material from a specialty native or tropical plant nursery.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension -- Erythrina species for Gulf Coast gardens
San Marcos Growers -- Erythrina x bidwillii
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew -- Erythrina hybrids
